name: Carlos Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a stockman at Valley Producers, a farmers' co-op, which means a group of local families own it together and hire people like me to work it. We've got a hundred and eighty dairy cows plus wheat and maize for feed. I start milking at five with Femi, the herd manager, then it's feeding, scraping out, checking for lame cows, and in the afternoon I'm usually on a tractor somewhere.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part and the worst part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is when a heifer I helped calve comes into the milking line for the first time, it's like seeing a kid start school. Worst part is the pay. Marta does part-time shifts at the care home on Station Road and between us we cover the mortgage, but there's nothing left at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, so it's a better calculator. I use one of those chat apps now and then to check a feed ration or tidy up an email to the vet, and that's about what I expected. I'd say we should get back to talking about wages instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays the same, which is good, and my pay stays bad, which isn't. The co-op board would stop dreaming about robot milkers for a while. Femi and I would keep doing the milking at five like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd keep using the chat app for the boring stuff, maybe get the co-op to use it for the herd records. I'd push the farm workers' branch of the union to go after a pay rise, since there's no robot excuse anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like a promise of rain that didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the board dreaming about robot milkers. Has that come up already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring a salesman came and did a whole talk in the canteen. Four robot units, about a hundred and fifty thousand each. The board said not yet, and Femi said 'not yet means yes later'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If wages are the issue, what pay rise would actually change things at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two more an hour would be the difference between Marta doing four shifts a week or three. That's one evening a week with the kids. I'd sell that to the union as a family issue, not just money.

S0.say: AI turning out to be a better calculator is about what he expected, since he already uses a chat app for feed rations and emails. He'd say it's time to get back to talking about wages.
S0.think: His job stays the same, which is good, and his pay stays poor, which isn't. The co-op board would stop dreaming about robot milkers for a while.
S0.do: Keeps using the chat app for routine paperwork and suggests it for the co-op's herd records. Pushes the farm workers' union branch for a pay rise of two an hour now that there's no robot excuse.
S0.feel: Calm, but a little flat, like a promised rain that never came.
S0.quote: Femi said 'not yet means yes later'.
S0.fieldNote: He is relaxed about technology in small doses and immediately turns the conversation to pay. The robot milker sales pitch from last spring is clearly still on his mind. He frames wages as family time, which is how he'd sell it to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op is exactly the right kind of farm to do this fairly, because it's owned by the families round here, not some fund in the city. I'd say, if robots come, the workers should get training and a share of what's saved. I'd post that on the co-op's members' group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think 'not yet' becomes yes, and the robot milkers come in within a couple of years. That's half my job. I'd probably still have a job, but it would be a different one, and maybe fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the co-op manager straight out to put me on the training when the robots come, first in line. I'd use the chat app more to learn how robot milkers work before they arrive, so I'm not starting from zero. And I'd get the union to negotiate that nobody's let go without retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. I've seen enough change on farms to know you don't stop it, you try to get on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Gerry, who's sixty-one and does the tractor work and can't read a screen without his glasses on his head. And honestly the lads on the arable side, because a self-driving combine doesn't need three of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'fewer of us' but also that you'd probably still have a job. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About seventy per cent sure. The robot still needs someone to fetch the cow that won't go in, and to clean the thing. It's the other thirty per cent that keeps me up a bit.

S1.say: The co-op, being owned by local families, is the right kind of farm to bring in robots fairly. Workers should get training and a share of what's saved.
S1.think: He expects robot milkers within a couple of years, taking half of what he does now. He'd probably keep a job, but a different one, with fewer people on the team.
S1.do: Asks the co-op manager to put him first in line for robot training and uses the chat app to learn about robot milkers before they arrive. Gets the union to negotiate retraining before anyone is let go.
S1.feel: Uneasy but okay, because he thinks you get on the right side of change rather than stopping it.
S1.quote: The robot still needs someone to fetch the cow that won't go in, and to clean the thing.
S1.fieldNote: He trusts the co-op structure to share gains, which reflects his progressive outlook. He puts a number on his own safety, seventy per cent, and is honest about the gap. His first worry is for older colleague Gerry and the arable crew, not himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the government has to step in, full stop. Some kind of basic income, and robots taxed so that the money goes back to the people who lost the work. I'd be on the members' group saying the co-op can't just go along with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too quick for the co-op to even hold a vote, never mind protect us. If a robot can do Femi's job and mine, the families who own the co-op will have to buy them or go bust against the big farms. I wouldn't blame them, and that's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut straight away: the car on finance goes back, no new phone for Luis. Marta would try to get full-time hours at the care home, because care work might last longer than farm work. I'd sign up with the union for whatever they're fighting for and put my name down for any government help the day it opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Proper stomach-ache alarmed. Two years is less time than our car loan has left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the conversation with Marta like that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit at the kitchen table after the kids are in bed and do the sums on the back of an envelope, like we did when Ana was born. She'd say 'we've done it before'. I'd say 'not like this' and then we'd stop talking for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't blame the co-op families. Isn't that a bit generous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I know them. Mrs Okafor who chairs the board milked her own cows until her knees went. If the choice is robots or losing the farm her grandad started, I'd pick robots too, and then I'd want the government to look after people like me.

S2.say: This is when government has to step in with something like a basic income, paid for by taxing robots. He'd say on the members' group that the co-op can't just go along with it.
S2.think: Two years is too quick for the co-op even to hold a vote, never mind protect workers. He thinks the owning families would have to buy robots or go bust, and he wouldn't blame them.
S2.do: Hands back the car on finance and cancels a new phone for his son straight away, while Marta looks for full-time care home hours. Backs the union's campaign and signs up for any government help the day it opens.
S2.feel: Alarmed to the point of a stomach-ache, because two years is shorter than the car loan.
S2.quote: Two years is less time than our car loan has left.
S2.fieldNote: His politics point to the government, not to his employer, whom he defends by name. The kitchen-table scene with Marta is the most personal moment so far. The car loan comparison shows how he measures time in debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so plan. Train workers on the robots, give us a stake, and get the government's support lined up before 2031, not after. I'd be saying it in the canteen and at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to learn something useful but not enough to pay off anything. I'd be forty-eight, still with a mortgage and Luis about to start college. It's a race I might just win if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the dairy robot technician course at the agricultural college in the evenings, two nights a week, if the co-op paid half. I'd put whatever I can aside, even thirty a week, into a savings pot. And I'd keep on at the union so there's a deal in place before the robots fully take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the useful kind. Like the week before a show when there's a lot to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the course helps you stay on, what happens when the AI can do the technician part too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's the same problem a few years later. But someone has to be there with the cows when it breaks, and I'd rather it was me than a man driving in from two hours away. I'm betting on being the person close by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save that thirty a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaway on Friday, that's twenty-five gone. Ana's swimming lessons I wouldn't touch. And I'd stop buying the farming magazine, I can read it at the co-op for free.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan, so the co-op and government should train workers, give them a stake and line up support before 2031. He'd say it in the canteen and at union meetings.
S3.think: Five years is enough to learn something useful but not to pay off debts, and his son would be starting college. He sees it as a race he might win if he starts now.
S3.do: Takes a dairy robot technician course at the agricultural college two evenings a week, asking the co-op to pay half. Saves thirty a week by cutting the Friday takeaway and keeps pressing the union for a deal.
S3.feel: Anxious in a useful way, like the busy week before a show.
S3.quote: I'm betting on being the person close by.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year window shifts him from defending his job to retraining for the nearest new one. He knows the technician role might also be automated but bets on being local and physical. His spending cuts are small and specific, and he protects his daughter's swimming lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and if we waste it, that's on the politicians, not on AI. I'd want farm workers on the committees that plan it. And I'd tell the younger ones at work to get trained up now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fifty-three when it lands. Ten years is time to get a skill and maybe pay a chunk off the house. I think I'd be all right, not comfortable, but all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd do the robot course and then a second one in farm electrics. I'd get on the union's working group on automation. And we'd talk to Luis about what he wants to study, because I don't want him walking into a job that's gone by the time he finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's like knowing a hard winter's coming but you've got time to get the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be on a farm by the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if there's a place. I don't mind if it's minding robots instead of cows, as long as I'm outdoors and near animals. I'd hate an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luis about farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the machines and the animals both, because the people who know both will be the last ones needed. He's thirteen and only wants to play football, so I'd tell him gently.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, and wasting it would be the politicians' fault, not AI's. Farm workers should sit on the planning committees, and young workers should train now.
S4.think: He'd be fifty-three when it lands, with time to gain a skill and pay down some of the mortgage. He expects to be all right, not comfortable.
S4.do: Takes the robot technician course and then a farm electrics course over the first few years. Joins the union's automation working group and talks with his son about what to study.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, like getting the hay in before a hard winter.
S4.quote: I don't mind if it's minding robots instead of cows, as long as I'm outdoors and near animals.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he sounds almost settled, mainly because the timeline fits his habit of adopting things once they're proven. He'd accept a changed role as long as it keeps him outdoors. His thoughts quickly go to his son's education.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, because there's no time for the co-op or the union to do anything. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, and the co-op paying for courses before the robots arrive, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Femi. He's been herd manager twenty years and he's the best stockman I've met, and he'd be the first to go because he's the most expensive. Whatever happens, I'd want someone to look after the Femis.

headlineQuote: Best part is when a heifer I helped calve comes into the milking line for the first time, it's like seeing a kid start school.
portrait: Carlos Santos is 43 and works as a stockman at Valley Producers, a dairy and crop co-op owned by local families, earning a low wage while his partner Marta works part-time at a care home. He leans left, trusts the union and believes in sharing the gains from machines. He uses AI tools now and then and accepts change once it's proven. In the mild scenarios he focuses on pay and on getting first in line for robot training. With AGI in two years he is alarmed and turns to government help, but with five or ten years he retrains as a robot technician and plans his son's education.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because neither the co-op nor the union would have time to protect workers.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income while people retrain, and the co-op paying for courses before the robots arrive rather than after.
